How the data is processed

Draft for version 2 of the database, not published yet. Built on 2026-11-10 from the build of version 2.

Steps

  1. Raw files, as published. Each dataset is compiled again from the files of its authors, with its metadata from anta_json (commit not recorded). Corrected files given by the authors replace the published ones where listed below.
  2. Depths. Travel times are converted to depths with the wave speed of the article, and the firn correction is added, only where the published depths have none (Cavitte_2020, Wang_2023). Elsewhere the depths stay as published, with the firn correction of their authors (table below).
  3. Lines. A line is one file of the database, named by its line ID. Lines are never cut. The points of a line are put in order along it where its layers were published in separate files. A line only lists the layers it has values of.
  4. Ice thickness, bed and surface elevation. Where a raw file gives two of the three, the third is computed (S = B + T). Where a line has none, they are taken from the Bedmap survey line of the same radar traces: the nearest Bedmap survey point, never the gridded Bedmap products (rules below).
  5. Where each value comes from. ICE_THK_SOURCE, BED_ELEV_SOURCE and SURF_ELEV_SOURCE, per point: 0 the published dataset, 1, 2, 3 a Bedmap1, Bedmap2 or Bedmap3 survey point, 4 computed from the two other published variables; missing where there is no value. BEDMAP_POINT_DIST: the distance to that Bedmap point.
  6. Platform and dating. Each line says whether its radar was airborne or ground-based (platform), and each layer how it was dated: the attributes dating method (ice-core or modelled), ice core and chronology of IRH_AGE, one value per layer. Both can be queried: db.query(platform="ground-based", dating_method="ice-core").

Ice thickness, bed and surface from Bedmap

  • Only Bedmap surveys of the same platform: airborne lines with the airborne surveys, ground-based lines with the ground surveys (and the seismic soundings). The radar on the ground traces other ice than an aircraft flying over it.
  • For each point, the nearest point of the Bedmap survey within 50 m. One survey per line, chosen by the most points matched (the newest generation when two are close): values are never mixed from two surveys.
  • The survey is only taken if its points are within 10 m of those of the line, on median: the same traces are 0 to 7 m apart, other flights over the same place 25 to 42 m. Exception: Siegert_2004, 50 m, whose flights Bedmap1 has in short pieces only (so its fill has gaps).
  • Published values are never replaced. A line with nothing missing is not changed.

The table comes with the next build of version 2.

Bedmap values left out

Each Bedmap survey was compared with the Bedmap3 grid. Values found wrong are left out of the Bedmap lines, so they never reach the isochrone lines, and the reason is in the attribute processing of their files:

  • NASA_2002_ICEBRIDGE_AIR_BM2: Surface and bed elevation of the published file left out: they are the distances from the aircraft down to the surface and the bed (the surface falls where the Bedmap3 surface rises), not elevations; the ice thickness agrees with Bedmap3.
  • NASA_2004_ICEBRIDGE_AIR_BM2: Surface and bed elevation of the published file left out: they are the distances from the aircraft down to the surface and the bed (the surface falls where the Bedmap3 surface rises), not elevations; the ice thickness agrees with Bedmap3.
  • NASA_2010_ICEBRIDGE_AIR_BM2: Surface and bed elevation of the published file left out: they are the distances from the aircraft down to the surface and the bed (the surface falls where the Bedmap3 surface rises), not elevations; the ice thickness agrees with Bedmap3.
  • PRIC_2016_CHA2_AIR_BM3: Three of its profiles left out (starting at x, y = 1829, -151; 1056, 228; 2197, 527 km): their surface is 700 to 2700 m below Bedmap3 and noisy from point to point, their thickness 700 to 1200 m off, unlike the other 110 profiles (within 30 m).

Where a Bedmap line has no surface (as these NASA surveys now), the 3D viewer draws it at the Bedmap3 surface.

Known issue, kept as published for now: BAS_2007_AGAP_AIR_BM2, line 69, whose last 240 km lie on the Ross Ice Shelf with the values of the plateau (surface 3,400 m): wrong positions, to report to the Bedmap team. No isochrone line is near it.
